lesson.title: Metaphase: Lining Up at the Center
lesson.summary: Metaphase is the stage of mitosis when spindle microtubules align all the duplicated chromosomes along the cell's equator, the metaphase plate, and verify their attachment before allowing separation to begin.
lesson.body:
By the time a cell reaches metaphase, every chromosome has been captured by the mitotic spindle that formed during prophase, and the defining event of this phase is getting all of them into position. Spindle microtubules extending from the two opposite poles pull and push each chromosome until it comes to rest along an imaginary plane, equally distant from both poles, called the metaphase plate. The result, at the height of metaphase, is a single orderly row of chromosomes stretched across the middle of the cell, each one attached to microtubules coming from both directions.

That dual attachment is not incidental, it is the entire point of metaphase. Each chromosome's two sister chromatids each have their own kinetochore, and correct alignment means one chromatid's kinetochore is attached to microtubules from one pole while its sister chromatid's kinetochore is attached to microtubules from the opposite pole. Before allowing the cell to proceed any further, a surveillance mechanism called the spindle assembly checkpoint verifies that every single chromosome has achieved this correct, dual attachment. If even one chromosome is unattached or attached incorrectly, the checkpoint halts the cycle until it is fixed.

This strict verification exists because metaphase is setting up an event that cannot be undone. Once the chromatids separate in the next phase, there is no way to reattach them or reverse a mistake. By insisting that every chromosome be correctly attached to microtubules from both poles before that separation begins, the spindle assembly checkpoint ensures that when the pull finally comes, each pole receives exactly one copy of every chromosome, no more and no less.
